paragraphs: Ordinary Bayes updating combines prior probabilities with a data likelihood to obtain posterior probabilities. This paper extends that operation to matrix representations: the prior becomes a symmetric positive definite matrix with trace one, and the likelihood is represented by a covariance matrix. When both matrices are diagonal, the proposed rule reduces to classical Bayes updating.

The extension changes how the overall evidence is calculated. Instead of averaging likelihoods under prior probabilities, it averages variances measured along the prior matrix's eigenvectors. The corresponding eigenvalues supply the averaging weights, while the covariance matrix determines the variance in each direction. This gives the matrix construction a concrete interpretation in terms of directions and uncertainty.

The authors also connect this calculation to quantum measurement and derive both updating rules from a minimum relative entropy principle. Classical relative entropy yields ordinary Bayes updating, while quantum relative entropy yields the matrix rule. The contribution is therefore a unified mathematical motivation for a broader update operation that retains the familiar diagonal case.
neurips-2005-a-bayes-rule-for-density-ma.tldr: The paper generalizes Bayes updating to density matrices while recovering classical Bayes rule for diagonal matrices.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the problem of detecting geographic concentrations of events, with emerging disease outbreaks as its application. A useful detector must recognize an unusual concentration quickly while avoiding too many false alarms. The authors introduce a Bayesian spatial scan statistic and compare it with the standard frequentist scan statistic for this task.

The proposed method changes the statistical approach used to assess spatial clusters. One practical advantage is that it does not require randomization testing. Eliminating that step makes the method much faster in the reported comparison. The authors also demonstrate increased power to detect clusters, meaning that the gain in runtime accompanies an improvement in detection capability.

The evaluation concerns prospective disease surveillance: identifying outbreaks as cases emerge. The Bayesian methods rapidly detect outbreaks while maintaining a low number of false positives in that evaluation. These findings matter because surveillance depends on both timely warnings and manageable false alarms; the reported results support the method on both dimensions.
neurips-2005-a-bayesian-spatial-scan-sta.tldr: A Bayesian spatial scan method improves cluster detection power and runtime while rapidly detecting disease outbreaks with few false positives in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Range images record distance, but the sensors considered here provide those measurements at a lower resolution than their accompanying camera images. The paper develops a Markov random field model that combines the two sources to produce more detailed depth images. The camera and range images are registered, so corresponding locations refer to the same scene.

The key observation is that boundaries in depth and boundaries in color tend to occur together. The model uses this relationship to bring information from the high-resolution camera image into the range reconstruction. The relationship is a tendency rather than an assertion that every color boundary must indicate a change in distance.

The resulting approach generates range images with both high resolution and low noise, and the authors report substantial improvement over existing range imaging technology. Its contribution is a concrete way to combine complementary measurements: range sensing supplies direct distance information, while the camera supplies finer spatial information that can help locate depth discontinuities.
neurips-2005-an-application-of-markov-ra.tldr: A Markov random field combines aligned camera and range images to produce higher-resolution, lower-noise depth estimates.

paragraphs: This paper studies semi-supervised learning methods that construct a kernel through an unsupervised spectral decomposition. The kernel provides the representation used for learning, while the spectral construction draws on structure in the data. The framework encompasses a class of earlier methods based on data graphs, allowing the authors to analyze them together.

The central theoretical result is a bound on generalization performance. The authors then choose the kernel design by minimizing that bound. This links the construction of the representation to a stated learning criterion: the selected design is optimal for the bound being minimized, rather than being presented as universally best for every prediction task.

The analysis explains why spectral kernel design can often improve predictive performance. Experiments illustrate the main consequences of the theory, connecting the mathematical treatment to observed behavior. The value of the work is both explanatory and prescriptive: it helps account for the success of existing graph methods and gives a principled objective for designing their kernels.
neurips-2005-analysis-of-spectral-kernel.tldr: The paper derives a generalization bound for spectral kernel methods and uses it to guide kernel design for semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer a probabilistic approach to classification, but their exact inference calculations cannot be carried out analytically in the setting considered here. Practical use therefore depends on approximations. This paper examines two such choices, Laplace's method and Expectation Propagation, to determine how well they support the quantities needed for classification.

The comparison focuses on marginal likelihood estimates and predictive performance. These are distinct concerns: an approximation must support predictions, while also estimating the evidence assigned to the observed data. By assessing both, the paper evaluates more than whether the methods merely produce usable class predictions in the experiments under study.

The authors provide a theoretical explanation for the superiority of Expectation Propagation over Laplace's method and corroborate that explanation empirically. They also compare Expectation Propagation with a sophisticated Markov chain Monte Carlo scheme and find it surprisingly accurate. Together, these results provide theoretical and experimental support for Expectation Propagation as an effective approximation for Gaussian process classification.
neurips-2005-assessing-approximations-fo.tldr: Theoretical and empirical comparisons favor Expectation Propagation over Laplace's method for Gaussian process classification.

paragraphs: Graph construction is a foundational choice in semi-supervised learning because it determines how the method represents relationships among data points. Different distance functions or neighborhood sizes produce different graphs. This paper proposes combining several such constructions through optimization, making the choice among graph representations part of the learning procedure itself.

Each candidate graph is associated with a basic graph kernel. The method then computes a combined kernel by solving an extended regularization problem that jointly minimizes over the data and the collection of graph kernels. The resulting notion of an optimal combination is tied to that objective, giving the combination a formal mathematical basis.

The authors report encouraging results on several optical character recognition tasks. Their candidate graphs vary in both distance function and the number of nearest neighbors used to build connections. These experiments support the practical promise of combining graph constructions, while the main methodological contribution is the joint optimization that determines how those alternatives enter the final kernel.
neurips-2005-combining-graph-laplacians-.tldr: The method learns a combined kernel from multiple graph constructions and shows encouraging results on character recognition tasks.

paragraphs: The paper explains spectral clustering and dimensionality reduction through diffusion on a graph. Starting from pairwise adjacency information, the authors define a distance between points using a diffusion process. This provides a probabilistic interpretation of the geometry represented by the graph and of the eigenvectors used to summarize it.

They show that a representation using the first few eigenvectors of the corresponding Markov matrix is optimal under a particular mean squared error criterion. The qualification matters: the result establishes optimality for the specified diffusion-based approximation objective. It supplies a mathematical reason for retaining those eigenvectors when building a low-dimensional representation.

A second connection assumes that points are randomly sampled from a density of the form p(x) = e^(-U(x)). Under this setup, the graph eigenvectors approximate eigenfunctions of a Fokker–Planck operator with potential 2U(x) and reflecting boundaries. Known properties of that continuous operator then help justify the success of spectral methods and explain empirical observations through characteristics of diffusion.
neurips-2005-diffusion-maps-spectral-clu.tldr: A diffusion interpretation connects spectral embeddings to a precise approximation objective and, under a sampling assumption, to continuous Fokker–Planck operators.

paragraphs: This paper connects two ways of describing classification problems: surrogate losses, which define penalties used in learning, and f-divergences, which measure differences between probability distributions. A general theorem establishes a correspondence between these objects. The result offers a shared mathematical language for studying choices that otherwise appear to belong to different parts of a learning problem.

The correspondence is constructive. The authors give procedures for finding the divergence associated with a surrogate loss and for finding all surrogate losses that realize a specified divergence. They also define universal equivalence among losses and their corresponding divergences, then establish conditions that are both necessary and sufficient for that equivalence.

These ideas apply when classification also requires decisions about experimental design. The authors use the theory to prove consistency for a classifier-learning procedure subject to decentralization requirements. The contribution therefore extends beyond translating between mathematical objects: the correspondence and equivalence results support a learning guarantee in a setting with constraints on how classification is organized.
neurips-2005-divergences-surrogate-loss-.tldr: The paper connects surrogate classification losses with f-divergences and uses that theory to prove consistency under decentralization requirements.

paragraphs: Direct policy gradient estimation provides an appealing way to learn behavior in reinforcement learning, but the resulting optimization can be difficult to control in practice. This paper targets that optimization difficulty. Its aim is to make policy gradient learning more robust and to improve how quickly the learning process converges.

The proposed approach uses stochastic meta-descent to adapt a gain vector, adjusting the scales of the optimization updates. The adaptation employs fast Hessian-vector products, which bring information about the curvature of the optimization problem into the update procedure. The method therefore acts on how policy learning proceeds, using an adaptive mechanism to address poorly behaved optimization.

In the reported experiments, the resulting algorithms outperform previously used online stochastic, offline conjugate, and natural policy gradient methods. These findings support the authors' claim that gain adaptation can improve robustness and convergence speed. The comparison is an experimental result for the studied algorithms and problems, providing evidence for the approach's practical usefulness.
neurips-2005-fast-online-policy-gradient.tldr: Stochastic meta-descent adapts policy gradient update gains, improving robustness and convergence speed in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper asks how reinforcement learning can explain the speed and intensity with which animals work for rewards. Free-operant conditioning experiments measure response rates, yet the existing models discussed by the authors lack a notion of vigor. This leaves them unable to address how motivational states such as hunger change the amount of work animals perform.

The proposed framework treats vigor as a choice governed by the costs and benefits of responding quickly. Motivation changes those factors and therefore shifts the preferred response rate. This gives a normative account of why an animal might work harder when hungry, including findings in which increased productivity extends to outcomes such as water.

The framework accounts for effects of motivation on response rates and several other classic findings. The authors further suggest that tonic dopamine may participate in the computation linking motivational state to optimal responding. That proposed neural role offers an explanation for complex effects of dopamine manipulation, while remaining a hypothesis about the underlying computation.
neurips-2005-how-fast-to-work-response-v.tldr: A reinforcement learning account treats response vigor as a cost-benefit choice and proposes a possible computational role for tonic dopamine.

paragraphs: The paper develops a probability distribution for models that describe objects through latent features without fixing a finite upper limit on the number of possible features. The mathematical representation is a binary matrix with finitely many rows and an unbounded number of columns. In this representation, rows correspond to objects and columns encode feature presence.

The distribution is defined over equivalence classes of these matrices and can serve as a prior for probabilistic feature models. The authors also identify a simple generative process that produces the same distribution over equivalence classes. They name this construction the Indian buffet process, providing a generative description of the proposed mathematical prior.

To demonstrate its use, the authors build an infinite latent feature model and derive a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for inference. They apply that algorithm to an image dataset. The contribution combines a prior for potentially unlimited feature representations, a process that generates it, and an inference procedure for a concrete model using it.
neurips-2005-infinite-latent-feature-mod.tldr: The Indian buffet process supplies a prior for latent feature models with an unbounded number of possible features.

paragraphs: Integrate-and-fire models are widely used to study spiking neurons, yet their simplicity raises questions about how faithfully they can reproduce real neuronal activity. This paper evaluates that issue using intracellular recordings from cortical pyramidal neurons. The authors develop a sequential procedure for quantitatively evaluating an effective integrate-and-fire-type model against those recordings.

The resulting model predicts the real neuron's spike train with high accuracy. In regimes resembling conditions in vivo, the predicted and recorded traces are almost indistinguishable, and a significant portion of spikes occur at the correctly predicted times. These findings demonstrate substantial predictive ability for the effective model in the conditions examined.

Slow processes, especially spike-frequency adaptation, are central to this result. The authors find them necessary for connecting model behavior across different driving regimes. The paper's claim of adequacy therefore concerns a model that incorporates adaptation: retaining this slow behavior allows a comparatively simple neuronal description to reproduce important aspects of the recorded activity.
neurips-2005-integrate-and-fire-models-w.tldr: An integrate-and-fire-type model predicts recorded neuronal activity accurately, with adaptation needed to connect behavior across driving regimes.

paragraphs: A dynamic texture models a video as a realization of a stochastic process evolving across space and time, specifically a linear dynamical system. The paper identifies a limitation of this representation: it cannot capture video containing multiple regions with distinct motion. Such video requires a model that can account for different motion patterns within the same sequence.

The authors introduce a layered dynamic texture model to address that problem. The layered formulation provides a way to represent multiple motion regions within the video model. They also develop a variant and present expectation-maximization algorithms for learning both formulations, supplying procedures for fitting the proposed representations from data.

The model is demonstrated on video segmentation and synthesis. These tasks examine complementary uses of the representation: separating a sequence into regions and generating video from a learned model. The reported efficacy supports the usefulness of the layered approach for handling distinct motions, while the learning algorithms make the proposed models operational for those tasks.
neurips-2005-layered-dynamic-textures-77.tldr: Layered dynamic textures extend video modeling to multiple regions with distinct motion and support both segmentation and synthesis.

paragraphs: Clustering methods can fit a model to each group or connect examples according to pairwise affinity. The paper seeks to combine the benefits of these approaches. Pairwise relationships can guide similar examples into the same cluster, while many applications also need an explicit prototype or model that describes each resulting group.

Affinity propagation learns a mixture model by repeatedly passing affinity messages. The authors also interpret the procedure as belief propagation in a graphical model that represents pairwise training-case likelihoods and the identification of cluster centers. This connects the message-passing process to a probabilistic formulation of the clustering problem.

The method is demonstrated on image-patch clustering for segmentation and on mixtures of gene expression models from microarray data. In these experiments, it finds better solutions than Gaussian mixtures, K-medoids, spectral clustering, and hierarchical clustering. It can also work with a specified number of clusters or determine that number automatically, giving the same approach two useful ways to organize the data.
neurips-2005-mixture-modeling-by-affinit.tldr: Affinity propagation learns mixture models through message passing and outperforms several clustering alternatives in the reported applications.

paragraphs: Non-Gaussian component analysis is a linear dimensionality reduction method built around a particular definition of irrelevant structure: Gaussian components are treated as uninteresting. The method seeks a lower-dimensional subspace containing the non-Gaussian components of high-dimensional data. This makes the choice of what to discard central to how the representation is constructed.

The authors formulate the problem in a general semi-parametric framework. By projecting out the Gaussian structure, they estimate the relevant non-Gaussian subspace. They also show that the estimation error tends to zero at a parametric rate, providing a statistical convergence result for recovering those components within the proposed framework.

Once extracted, the components can be used for visualization, clustering, denoising, or classification. A numerical study demonstrates the method's usefulness. The approach matters because it offers a common preprocessing representation for several analysis tasks, with relevance defined through departures from Gaussian structure and supported by a theoretical result about the accuracy of subspace estimation.
neurips-2005-non-gaussian-component-anal.tldr: NGCA estimates a non-Gaussian subspace by removing Gaussian structure and establishes parametric-rate convergence of its estimation error.

paragraphs: The paper studies decision rules that compare objects by checking cues in an ordered sequence. In these lexicographic strategies, cue ordering is central to the quality of the decisions. The motivating example is take-the-best, a fast and frugal heuristic intended to make effective decisions when computational resources are limited.

The authors investigate how difficult it is to approximate the best possible ordering of cues. The supplied abstract states that no efficient algorithm can approximate the optimum within any constant factor if P = NP. That is the condition as supplied; the computational claim must be read together with its stated condition rather than as an unconditional impossibility.

The paper also develops a simple greedy algorithm for constructing lexicographic strategies and derives tight bounds on its performance ratio. It proves that this algorithm performs better than take-the-best. The work therefore examines both the difficulty of obtaining good cue orderings and a concrete alternative with a stronger proven performance guarantee than the motivating heuristic.
neurips-2005-on-the-accuracy-of-bounded-.tldr: The paper analyzes approximation of cue orderings and proves that a new greedy strategy performs better than take-the-best.

paragraphs: Kernel principal component analysis estimates spaces that capture structure in a kernel representation of data. This paper asks how accurately those spaces themselves are estimated. That focus differs from assessing reconstruction error, which concerns how well a representation reproduces data rather than how close the estimated eigenspaces are to their underlying targets.

The authors provide a non-asymptotic statistical analysis, so their result concerns finite amounts of data rather than only a limiting regime. They prove an upper bound on eigenspace approximation error. The bound depends on the spacing between eigenvalues, making spectral separation an explicit part of the accuracy analysis.

A notable feature is that the bound does not depend on the dimensionality of the eigenspace. From this result, the authors infer stability properties for the estimated spaces. The contribution is a direct theoretical account of the reliability of kernel-PCA eigenspaces, complementing analyses that judge the method through the reconstruction quality of its output.
neurips-2005-on-the-convergence-of-eigen.tldr: The paper bounds kernel-PCA eigenspace estimation error using eigenvalue spacing without dependence on eigenspace dimensionality.

paragraphs: Visual search requires selecting cues that distinguish a target from surrounding clutter. This paper asks whether the human visual system makes that selection optimally. The authors define an optimal strategy by maximizing the signal-to-noise ratio between the target and distractors, turning a question about attention into a specific mathematical objective.

The resulting strategy accounts for several established aspects of search behavior. These include how easily targets can be distinguished from distractors, uncertainty about target features, variation among distractors, and linear separability. Addressing these effects through one objective gives the theory a common explanation for several influences on cue selection.

The theory also produces a new prediction, which the authors verify in psychophysical experiments with human participants. They interpret the findings as direct experimental evidence that people select visual cues to maximize target-versus-clutter signal-to-noise ratio. The result ties the proposed optimality criterion to measured behavior, supporting it as an explanation of cue choice in the studied visual search setting.
neurips-2005-optimal-cue-selection-strat.tldr: A signal-to-noise-maximizing cue selection theory explains visual search effects and receives support from a verified human behavioral prediction.

paragraphs: Active learning aims to reduce the cost of training by selecting which examples to use. This paper introduces KQBC, an algorithm designed to make selective sampling practical for large-scale problems. It builds on Query By Committee, whose sampling step can be computationally expensive and therefore obstruct its use at scale.

KQBC addresses that bottleneck by projecting onto a low-dimensional space and performing sampling there. The sampling procedure uses a hit-and-run random walk. Moving the costly operation into this smaller space is the central computational change, allowing the algorithm to retain a selective-sampling approach while overcoming the expensive step identified in the original method.

The algorithm also supports kernels, providing a way to extend Query By Committee to nonlinear problems. The authors demonstrate successful applications to artificial problems and a real-world problem. Together, the low-dimensional sampling construction and kernel extension broaden the practical scope of the method, addressing both computational scale and the kinds of relationships the learner can represent.
neurips-2005-query-by-committee-made-rea.tldr: KQBC makes Query By Committee more practical through low-dimensional sampling and adds kernel support for nonlinear learning.

paragraphs: The paper explores a possible computational role for top-down connections in vision: representing relationships between wholes and their parts. The analyzed network has one layer for parts and another for wholes, with bidirectional interactions between layers and lateral inhibition within each layer. Evidence can therefore travel from parts to wholes and from wholes back to parts.

Within identified parameter regimes, this interaction supports several behaviors. A recognized whole can suppress parts that do not belong to it and fill in parts that are missing. Conversely, the network can decline to recognize a whole when the active parts fail to match a stored part-whole relationship.

The authors use the theory of permitted and forbidden sets to determine parameter regimes supporting these capabilities. They illustrate the behaviors by recreating an interactive activation model. The contribution is a mathematical account of how recurrent connectivity can enforce structural consistency during recognition, offering a computational hypothesis for top-down connections rather than establishing their biological function.
neurips-2005-representing-part-whole-rel.tldr: A recurrent network can enforce part-whole consistency, complete missing parts, and reject incompatible wholes in identified parameter regimes.

paragraphs: Choosing a biological experiment through optimization requires a model, but the model's parameter estimates may initially be poor. The paper identifies this as a source of brittleness in classical optimal experiment design. A design selected using inaccurate nominal parameters can perform poorly, and computational constraints create an additional obstacle to using such methods in practice.

The authors propose a robust design method based on a semidefinite programming relaxation. This provides an optimization-based approach intended to address both robustness and computational efficiency. The central motivation is to choose experiments that remain useful when the parameter estimates informing the design are unreliable.

They apply the method to experiment design for a complex calcium signal transduction pathway. In this application, the robust design produces better parameter estimates than an optimal design based on the nominal model. The result illustrates why accounting for uncertainty in the starting estimates can improve the eventual information gained from an experiment, even when the competing design is optimal under its assumed parameters.
neurips-2005-robust-design-of-biological.tldr: A robust experiment design method improves parameter estimation over a nominally optimal design in a calcium signaling application.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how the appearance of a natural scene relates statistically to its depth, and how that relationship changes with scale. The practical goal is to enhance a low-resolution range image using a full-resolution intensity image of the same scene. The analysis asks which information in appearance can help recover finer depth structure.

Using their findings, the authors extend an existing method called shape recipes. They compare the extension with the original technique using images and laser scans of real scenes. The extension achieves a reported two-fold improvement, providing empirical support for using the observed scale-dependent relationships to improve range reconstruction.

The paper also examines linear shape-from-shading filters learned from natural scenes. It finds that ideal filters may obtain even more of their strength from shadows than from traditional linear-Lambertian shading cues. This suggests that their effectiveness can reflect information carried by shadows, broadening the interpretation of what a learned shading-based predictor is exploiting.
neurips-2005-scaling-laws-in-natural-sce.tldr: Scale-dependent image-depth statistics improve a range-enhancement method, while learned shading filters may draw substantial strength from shadows.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a spectral clustering method that lets users incorporate prior knowledge about cluster sizes. Its objective, size regularized cut, combines similarity between clusters with a regularization term measuring the relative sizes of two clusters. The formulation makes size information an explicit part of deciding how to partition the data.

The authors prove that finding a partition minimizing this objective is NP-complete. They therefore propose an approximation algorithm for a relaxed version of the problem, expressed as an eigenvalue problem. This provides a computational route to using the objective while distinguishing the relaxed solution from an exact solution of the original partitioning problem.

Evaluations on different datasets show that the method is not sensitive to outliers and performs better than normalized cut in those comparisons. The contribution is a clustering criterion that combines similarity structure with size expectations, together with an approximation procedure and empirical evidence that the resulting partitions can improve on a standard spectral clustering approach.
neurips-2005-size-regularized-cut-for-da.tldr: Size regularized cut incorporates cluster-size knowledge into spectral clustering and improves on normalized cut in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a Gaussian process regression model whose covariance is controlled by the locations of a set of pseudo-input points. Their locations are learned through gradient-based optimization, together with the covariance hyperparameters. Using a small set of these points provides a sparse representation for regression on a larger collection of real observations.

With M pseudo-inputs and N real data points, the stated training cost is O(M²N), and prediction costs O(M²) per test case. The authors also interpret the method as Bayesian regression with a particular form of input-dependent noise. They discuss its close relationships with other sparse Gaussian process approaches.

Experiments on large datasets directly compare the method with alternative sparse approaches. The authors show that it can match full Gaussian process performance with small M and significantly outperform the alternatives in that very sparse regime. The result supports learning pseudo-input locations as a way to retain predictive performance while using a compact covariance representation.
neurips-2005-sparse-gaussian-processes-u.tldr: Learning pseudo-input locations yields sparse Gaussian process regression that can match full-model performance with a small representation.

paragraphs: Many subspace methods represent an image by flattening its pixels into one long vector. This paper proposes Tensor Subspace Analysis, which instead treats an image as a second-order tensor, retaining its matrix form. That representation allows relationships among rows and among columns to be characterized naturally within the learning method.

TSA learns a lower-dimensional tensor subspace intended to capture the intrinsic local geometry of the tensor space. The motivation connects to earlier observations that image variation, particularly for faces under changing lighting, can be represented effectively in low-dimensional spaces. TSA brings the image's two-dimensional organization into the construction of such a representation.

The authors compare TSA with principal component analysis, linear discriminant analysis, and locality preserving projection on two standard databases. The reported experiments show higher recognition rates and much greater efficiency for TSA. These results support preserving matrix structure as a useful design choice for the evaluated recognition tasks, alongside the method's explicit treatment of local geometry.
neurips-2005-tensor-subspace-analysis-f0.tldr: Tensor Subspace Analysis preserves image matrix structure and achieves better recognition and efficiency than three vector-based methods in the reported comparisons.
